1.pericope_label: David’s purpose to build, and the word that came to Nathan the same night

schools.summary: Ellicott separates the order of the book from the order of events: in both texts this story naturally follows the removal of the ark, although the events themselves appear to belong to a later period of David’s reign, when the Lord had given him rest round about from all his enemies, while the promise about his seed indicates some time before the birth of Solomon, so that the date cannot be more exactly determined. He finds the chronicler’s hand in two words: where this account names David three times in as many clauses Samuel has simply the king, and the chronicler loves the name of his ideal sovereign; and where this account has God, Samuel has Jehovah, though the same verses had just said the ark of God. The phrase the same night he takes to indicate a dream as the method of communication. On the refusal itself he would render more pointedly than the English, that it is not thou that shalt build me the house to dwell in, noting that Samuel puts the same thing as a question implying its own denial, and explaining the definite article by the chronicler’s vantage point, since he is thinking of the famous temple of Solomon. Over Nathan’s first and hastier answer he pauses on the organ named, that according to Hebrew ideas the heart was the seat of the mind and the will as well as of the emotions, a conception he thinks better than what passed for anatomy long after, since even Aristotle, seven centuries later than David, supposed the brain to be merely a kind of cooling counterpoise to the heat of the liver.

Clarke sets the chapter out as an argument: David consults Nathan about building a temple, God sends him an answer by Nathan informing him that Solomon shall build the house, and David receives the divine purpose with humility and joy and gives God praise. For the detail of it he refers the reader to his notes on the parallel in Samuel, where he says everything recorded in this chapter is amply detailed.

Henry takes the opening for an example of how desirous and solicitous good people should be to serve the interests of God’s kingdom in the world to the utmost of their capacity. David could not be easy in a house of cedar while the ark was lodged within curtains, for the concerns of the public should always be near our hearts, and what pleasure can we take in our own prosperity if we see not the good of Jerusalem? He presses the contrast with what a man newly advanced to wealth and power might have been expected to ask: not what he shall do for his children to get portions for them, nor what he shall do to fill his coffers and enlarge his dominions, but what he shall do for God.

debates.question: Is the refusal a statement or a question?

positions.view: A statement here, and better rendered "it is not thou that shalt build"; Samuel asks it as a question implying denial

outliers.claim: Alone in observing that the chronicler writes David three times where Samuel writes "the king", and in explaining the definite article of "the house" by the later fame of Solomon’s temple.
Alone in reading the opening as a rebuke to the ambitions a newly prosperous man might have entertained instead.

7.pericope_label: I took thee from the sheepcote: the promise of a name, a place for Israel, and a house for David

schools.summary: Ellicott finds the force of the opening in a pronoun, which is emphatic — I it was who took thee from the pasture — and notes that where this account has from following the sheep the Hebrew reads from behind, Samuel preserving the older form of the preposition. More consequentially he corrects a tense: where the English has that God has made David a name like the name of the great men of the earth, he would render it as a promise still to come, and I will make thee; and he identifies those great men as the sovereigns of Egypt and Babylon, of Tyre, and of the Hittite states. The cutting off of David’s enemies he refers not merely to the death of Saul and the overthrow of his house but to the successful conclusion of wars recorded in the chapters following. The promise of a settled place he takes of a tenure never yet secure, since although Israel had effected a settlement in Canaan the history seems to show that down to the times of David the tribal boundaries were subject to great fluctuation and the inroads of surrounding peoples made their hold very uncertain; he notes that the Hebrew keeps Israel singular throughout where the English has the plural, and glosses the phrase in their place as in his own stead or fixed habitation, comparing our own homestead and farmstead. He complains besides of the verse division, that the clause about the days of the judges ought never to have been separated from what precedes, which it properly concludes. Of the manner of David’s death he observes that the phrase runs literally to go with thy fathers, an unusual expression where Samuel has the ordinary thou shalt lie down with thy fathers, and he judges the introductory phrase of that verse to be wanting in Samuel and probably to be supplied there from the Greek. On the promise of the throne he keeps to the comparison, that the pronoun is again emphatic, that where this account has build me an house Samuel has for my name, and that his throne stands here for Samuel’s throne of his kingdom, which he calls a characteristic abridgment. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the unusual phrase is used of going the way of death and is similar to the phrase about going the way of all the world, but make the sharper claim that this form is the more primitive of the two and that Samuel’s familiar lying down with the fathers is the later and more usual idiom.

Clarke refers the promise of a settled place much further back than Ellicott does, taking the children of wickedness who shall waste them no more to mean that Israel shall never again be brought into servitude as they were when they sojourned in Egypt. On the promise of a throne for ever he reads past the wording to the person, holding that David was a type of Christ and that concerning him the prophecy is literally true, with the prophet’s words about the increase of government and peace pointing the same way; and of the mercy that shall not be taken away he says plainly that God will not cut off this family from the throne as he cut off that of Saul before him. Wesley answers a question the others do not raise, whether David must think his purpose vain and the reward of it lost: no, for it being God’s own act that prevented the execution, he shall be as fully recompensed as if the thing had been done.

debates.question: What does the promise of a settled place answer to?

positions.view: A tenure never yet secure: fluctuating tribal boundaries and the inroads of surrounding peoples down to David’s time
The servitude in Egypt, which shall never be repeated

debates.question: Which text preserves the older idiom for dying?

positions.view: Chronicles: "to go with thy fathers" is the more primitive, Samuel’s "lie down with thy fathers" the more usual
Notes only that the phrase is unusual here and ordinary in Samuel

outliers.claim: Alone in claiming that the later book here preserves the more primitive idiom, against the usual assumption that Samuel is the older text throughout.
Alone in reading the promise of the throne as literally true of Christ, of whom David was a type.
Alone in asking whether David loses the reward of a purpose God himself prevented, and answering that he is recompensed as if it had been done.

16.pericope_label: David sits before the LORD: who am I, and what is mine house, that thou hast brought me hitherto?

schools.summary: Henry announces his method before using it: the prayer was largely observed on the parallel in Samuel, so that here he will note only those few expressions in which this record differs from that one and has something added to it. The difference he fastens on is a change of mood, that what stands there as a question, whether this is the manner of men, appears here as an acknowledgment that God has regarded David according to the estate of a man of high degree — God having made him a great man and then treated him accordingly. Of the prayer as a whole he observes how humbly David abases himself and acknowledges his own unworthiness, how highly he advances the name of God and admires his condescending grace and favour, with what devout affections he magnifies the God of Israel and what a value he has for the Israel of God, and with what assurance he builds upon the promise and with what lively faith he puts it in suit; by faith, he adds, David receives the promises and embraces them and is persuaded of them, as the patriarchs did.

Wesley reproduces Henry’s closing passage on the prayer almost word for word, down to the petition that the Lord would enable us all thus to seek him, so that the two are not independent witnesses here and are not presented as such. Clarke answers the question of the prayer in a single line of self-abasement, that David asks what his house is because he is not of any regal family and has no natural right at all to the throne.

Ellicott works the same obscure clause as Henry but from the Hebrew, and finds it simply obscure, noting that Samuel has the plainer and shorter reading, that this is the law of man, and that the word for law has been supposed to mean manner or custom in this place. On the opening question he observes that Samuel uses the longer form of the pronoun where this account has the shorter, and that where this account addresses God as Jehovah Elohim, Samuel has the form meaning my Lord Jehovah, which he judges the more original of the two; and he draws out the courtesy of that address, that David calls God my Lord just as God in the earlier verses had called David my servant, comparing the frequent style of the Assyrian kings, who speak of their wars as undertaken in the service of the gods their lords. The sitting before the Lord he places in the tent of the ark. At the following verse he proposes two emendations and is candid that they are emendations: Samuel has the word for speak which this account omits, and the word here translated for the honour may itself be a corruption of that very word; while the phrase of thy servant stands in the accusative and should in his judgment be struck out as a mistaken repetition of the same word at the end of the verse.

debates.question: What is to be made of the obscure clause about the estate of a man of high degree?

positions.view: Samuel’s question has here become an acknowledgment: God made him a great man and then treated him accordingly
The Hebrew is obscure; Samuel is plainer, and the word for "law" may mean manner or custom

outliers.claim: Alone in comparing David’s address to the style of the Assyrian kings, and alone in proposing that "for the honour" is a corruption of the word for "to speak".
Alone in stating a collation method for the Chronicles parallel, confining himself to what this record adds to the account in Samuel.

20.pericope_label: There is none like thee: Israel the one redeemed nation, and the prayer that the word be established

schools.summary: Ellicott distinguishes two words the English blurs: where the question runs what one nation in the earth is like thy people Israel, he would render who is like thy people Israel, a single and isolated race upon the earth, separating the term meaning a race, a people united by common blood and speech and country, from the term meaning a political community or state owning one sovereign. In the same verse he records a variant of some weight, that where this account says which God went to redeem to himself as a people, Samuel has the plural, which gods went, so that the chronicler’s text reads as a correction of the older one; the making of a name he takes to mean for God himself. Twice he suspects the text of damage or expansion: at the verse about God’s giving Israel to himself for a people, where Samuel has a verb meaning confirmed it, he judges our reading probably the result of partial obliteration; and at the next petition he notes that the doubled let it even be established is wanting in Samuel altogether, then observes that the words let be are not in the Hebrew, so that the clause about the house of David may not be a petition at all but part of what men are to say hereafter in praise of God. On a phrase he calls unique in Hebrew he renders that David hath found his heart, explaining it as having taken courage, the noun being expressed in Samuel and omitted here, and gives the preceding clause literally as God having uncovered the ear of his servant where Samuel has the more usual form. In the closing verses he finds the chronicler turning request into accomplished fact, rendering the last petition not as a request that it may please God to bless but as a statement that he has willed to bless, and for thou blessest as for thou hast blessed, remarking that Samuel is as usual the fuller of the two and that the chronicler drops the clause which follows there, that God’s words become truth.

Clarke twice prefers the Targum’s expansion to the bare Hebrew: on the unique phrase about finding the heart he thinks the Targum expresses the full sense, that thy servant hath found an opening of mouth that he might pray before thee; and on the closing blessing, that God begins to bless the house of his servant and therefore it shall be blessed for ever. At the end of the chapter he states his own practice outright, asking the reader to refer to his notes on the parallel in Samuel for the many particulars belonging to these places, which he says it would answer no good purpose to repeat here. Wesley closes on the title itself, that God is really to his people what he has styled himself, their God, having taken such care of them and shown such mercy and truth to them as fully answered that name.

debates.question: How should the unique phrase about finding the heart be rendered?

positions.view: He hath found his heart, that is, hath taken courage; the noun is expressed in Samuel
With the Targum: he hath found an opening of mouth, that he might pray

debates.question: Is the clause about the house of David a petition?

positions.view: Perhaps not: "let be" is absent from the Hebrew, so it may be part of what men are to say in praise of God

outliers.claim: Alone in reporting that Samuel has a plural "which gods went" where this account has the singular, and alone in attributing a reading here to partial obliteration of the text.
Alone in stating explicitly that he will not repeat on the Chronicles parallel what he has already written on Samuel.
